reception.text: Roosevelt's call, three weeks earlier, to take over Hawaii's lighthouses ran across page one of the Hawaiian Star the afternoon his annual message was delivered.

political_impact.text: The Light-House Board was directed to take charge of the Hawaiian service the day after the signing, and the federal service took over the work on January 1, 1904.
political_impact.source: Report of the Light-House Board, 1904, p. 285; Annual Report of the Light-House Board, fiscal 1906, p. 134

political_impact.text: The Board added the Hawaiian Islands to its Twelfth District and assigned a naval officer and an Army engineer to duty there.
political_impact.source: Report of the Light-House Board, 1904, p. 285

political_impact.text: The Board's first survey found some lights to be little more than household lamps; Lahaina's was two ordinary kitchen lamps, hard to tell from the lights of the town.
political_impact.source: Report of the Light-House Board, 1904, pp. 285–287

political_impact.text: A bill to reimburse the Territory, which had spent about $501.90 a month on the lights, was before the House Committee on Claims by early 1906.
political_impact.source: Annual Report of the Light-House Board, fiscal 1906, p. 134

political_impact.text: Congress repaid the Territory $23,393.69 for keeping up its lights from annexation until the federal Board took over.

legacy.text: Federal control brought a wave of construction: at least fifteen lights were built in the islands between 1906 and 1920.
Makapuʻu Point Light on Oahu, funded in 1906, was first lit on October 1, 1909, with a twelve-foot hyperradiant Fresnel lens, the largest size ever made.
legacy.source: Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1910, p. 508; LighthouseFriends

legacy.text: The Molokaʻi Light at Kalaupapa, the tallest tower in Hawaii, was first lit on September 1, 1909, at a cost of $59,977.04.
legacy.source: Reports of the Department of Commerce and Labor, 1910, p. 508

today.name: U.S. Coast Guard aids to navigation in Hawaii
today.note: The Light-House Board's duties passed to the Bureau of Lighthouses in 1910 and to the Coast Guard in 1939.

later_actions.text: Congress replaced the Light-House Board with a Bureau of Lighthouses.
Reorganization Plan No. II consolidated the Bureau of Lighthouses into the U.S. Coast Guard.

uncertain: How Honolulu papers greeted the proclamation itself in late December 1903 and early January 1904 has not been checked.
A Hawaiian Gazette item of May 6, 1904, seems to say lighthouse work was to wait on the Attorney General; the legal question is not known.
